dossier.public_summary: The dip looks shallow and flat but its depth jumps by about 300% between sectors and between individual transits, with a few very deep transits driving the detection. The light also wobbles at the same 4.03-day period outside the dip and shows a secondary dip, all centered on the target star itself. Together this is best explained by a blended or spot-affected binary/variability signal, not a small planet.

reasons.why: Depth changes by factor ~300 between sectors (ppm per_sector 800,1189,242,8,353,61,81). Positive evidence for blended/instrument/variability origin, not a constant planet depth.
Individual transits are inconsistent; top transits are ~4x mean (e.g. 1757, 1427, 1450, 1256, 1340 ppm) indicating outliers drive signal, not a repeatable planet.
Depth changes not only between sources but within same source (SPOC 2-min p_constant 5.728935904884914e-06, TESS-SPOC p_constant 3.7311299461562495e-08), ruling out calibration differences.

On-target, flat-bottom (shape v_sigma -1.993) and no odd/even difference (diff_sigma 0.5034) alone cannot earn a planet because duration is ~1.6x central with stellar density mismatch, there is a secondary at phase 0.5505 and large out-of-transit swing at same period, plus strong depth variability — consistent with a grazing / blended evolved binary or spot-induced signal, not a planet despite small size (rp_rearth 1.867).
